image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Dumbbell chart (paired dot plot comparing two groups across categories).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- Categories listed on the y-axis  
- Two colored dots per category connected by a horizontal line to show comparison between groups  
- No faceting or stacking

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College choice factor (e.g., affordable tuition, safe campus, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Relative importance | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Respondent group (16- to 19-year-olds vs recent college graduates) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of dots (orange vs teal) |
| Difference between the two groups for each factor | Quantitative | Horizontal distance between paired dots; connecting line length |

comments.raw_comment: I notice in the graph that financial factors appear to be the most important for both 16-19 year-olds and college grads. Affordable tuition and income potential have the greatest relative importance for both groups. For 16-19 year-olds, the school type (public/private) is the least important factor and varsity sports importance is the least important factor for college grads. I also notice that the factors with the greatest difference in importance between 16-19 year-olds and college grads are small class sizes and distance to family. For distance to family, the relative importance is about 1/4 less than it is for 16-19 year-olds. For small class sizes, the relative importance is around 1/3 lower for 16-19 year-olds than it is for graduates. I wonder why college graduates value being near family less than 16-19 year-olds. I wonder if this is because college graduates have become accustomed to living away from family and are now more comfortable or adjusted, and thus value distance to family/hometown less. Being a college student personally, I can relate to this and I believe those around me prioritize the same factors outlined in this, namely college affordability and income potential, as these can directly influence an individuals choice to attend a particular school or pursue a particular degree. How University Priorities Shift Before and After College

comments.raw_comment: From the graph, I noticed that “Affordable tuition” is the criterion that’s most prioritized for both high school students and college graduates, with graduates placing slightly higher importance on it. This indicates a shared concern over the financial burden of education. The gap in priorities is noticeable in the criteria of proximity to family or hometown and class sizes, with younger students placing more emphasis on family and older students placing more emphasis on quality of education. This indicates that as students mature and experience college life, their perspective on values shifts, showed by gaining appreciation for independence and personalized attention that smaller classes provide. I wonder how representative this data is across different demographics and if these priorities shift with cultural background, economic status, or region. I wonder where the surveyed 2,000 young people between the ages of 16 and 19 and the other 2,000 college graduates between the ages of 22 and 30 came from (specific city/state/county). As a college student myself, within a community that student debt is common, the importance of affordable tuition resonates deeply. The preference for small class sizes aligns with my personal educational experience at Cal Poly, where engagement and personalized feedback have been beneficial. A catchy headline that captures what’s going on in this graph is "Dollars and Diplomas: Students Share Stance on the Price of Learning".

comments.raw_comment:
I've noticed that affordable tuition stands out as the top priority for recent college graduates and 16-19 year olds alike, which makes perfect sense considering the aversion to attending an unaffordable college. Additionally, it's notable that 16-19 year olds place greater emphasis on proximity to family or hometown when choosing a college. Understandably, embarking on such a significant life transition prompts a desire to remain connected to familiar surroundings. In contrast, college graduates are more seasoned and accustomed to the college environment.
It's intriguing to ponder how long it takes for 16-19 year olds to adjust to college life and reassess their priorities, particularly regarding proximity to family or hometown. Personally, I can relate to this experience, as I, too, initially hesitated to venture far from home for college. The first few weeks away from my accustomed lifestyle were met with skepticism, yet over time, I adapted and discovered newfound independence.
A compelling headline capturing this transition could be "Pre-College vs. Post-College Priorities: Navigating the Shift."

comments.raw_comment: As a college student, this graph comparing what high school students and recent grads prioritize in choosing a college is eye-opening. Affordability and future income potential dominate for both, which makes sense but is also concerning. High schoolers care way more about being close to home, while grads value small class sizes - perspectives that seem to shift after experiencing college firsthand. I wonder if grads had some huge impersonal lectures that made them appreciate smaller discussions and professor relationships. As someone still in college, this makes me reflect on how my own priorities have evolved and will likely keep changing. A headline could be: "College Priorities: How Perspectives Shift from Application to Graduation." Overall, this shows the value of colleges connecting applicants with recent alumni insights. It has me thinking more deeply about what factors will matter most to me by the time I graduate.

The first thing I notice is that the gap between 16-19 year-olds prioritizing "near family or hometown" more than recent college grads. It stuck out to me because after going to college myself, I felt I enjoyed the convenience of being able to drive home, as opposed to being forced to fly. It seems like before college, people may find it scary to go so far from home for the first time. After college, it seems less scary to move away from your family. One thing I wonder is why there is a gap between "whether the school is public or private" between the college grads and 16- to 19-year-olds. Comparatively, they both feel nearly the same about affordable tuition. Since private schools tend to cost more than in-state public schools, I wonder if both groups surveyed had the financial aspect in mind when considering public vs private schools. I also wonder if one group preferred public schools or private schools more than the other.
This relates to me as someone who went to a school by almost complete chance, and realized that things I thought were important at first are less important now that I'm in college. I think a good headline for this graph might be "Change in Priorities: What College Grads Would Prioritize When Looking for a College"

comments.raw_comment:
What I Noticed

I noticed that 16-19 year olds and recent college graduates share the same perspective on which matters the most during college. Both groups see affordable tuition as the most significant, followed by graduate's potential for higher income. I also noticed the wide gap between the responses of the two groups when it comes to the importance of class sizes. Compared to 16-19 year olds, recent graduates see more importance in class sizes, which would make sense. Most college students would understand the long wait during office hours.

What I Wonder

I wonder if 16-19 year olds have changed their perspective on the importance of class size after attending college.

How does this relate to you and your community?

As a current college student, I would say reports like these would be beneficial and informative to incoming college students when choosing their university. Looking back, I probably would have had similar priorities to 16-19 year olds.

Headline

The College I Wish I Chose - Learning From Graduates

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed was the two largest gaps between the college hopefuls and the graduates. I think it makes a lot of sense that graduates would value being closer home less compared to the hopefuls. The hopefuls will most likely want to hold onto the friends that they have already made in high school and be scared of becoming more independent which is why they would want to stay close to home, however the graduates, after already going through college have already made new friends and have become independent, so they realized that being away from their hometown might have actually been a good thing. The other great difference comes with valuing small classes. It also makes a lot of sense that high schoolers, who probably haven't experienced big lecture classes, wouldn't value the small class sizes as much because they don't know. In the case for the graduates, because they already went through college, they were able see why having small classes is nice relative to big lecture classes. One thing I wonder is if the students they surveyed were just students from the United States. I would be interested in learning if this graph reflects students internationally. As a current college student, I can most definitely reflect a lot of what the graduates value, especially the small class sizes. A title I would give this graph is "A Reflection of Priorities, What do you Value?"

comments.raw_comment: It seems like there are three categories where the 16-19 year olds and 22-30 year olds tend to agree the most. First, affordable tuition is highly important to both age groups (above 4x relative importance). This makes sense for those considering college, as they would most likely want to attend a school that is affordable for them or their families. This is similar for those who had attended college and may want to go to graduate school or those who simply want their children’s college tuition to be reasonably priced as well. In addition to tuition, it looks like graduates’ higher income potential as well as racial and ethnic diversity closely align in importance between both age groups. In terms of the college being near family/hometown and class sizes, this is where the groups differ the most in their opinions. I wonder who the survey targeted. Was this a convenience sample? A random sample? Can we make generalizations about a larger population with this sample? I’m currently a college student finishing up my third year, so it’s interesting to see how graduates’ opinions change after attending college. I wonder if my opinions will be any different as well. As of now, I would highly consider higher income potential, racial and ethnic diversity, and the college having a safe campus if I had to make a decision on what school to go to. A catchy headline could be: “Decisions, decisions: How opinions of college considerations change before and after attending university”

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that for both 16-19 year olds and recent college graduates, the consensus most important aspect of choosing a college is the tuition fees and how affordable they are. I also notice that the biggest difference in opinions occur for class sizes. Graduated students appreciated the idea of smaller classes while the college students to be accept the idea of larger class and lecture halls. I notice that for graduate students, being close to family or a hometown is much less important. I think this is because when first leaving the house, the idea of being independent can be scary for 16 to 19 year olds which could result in timidness when thinking about going far from home.

I wonder if the priority of having a safe campus will ever over take affordable tuition as the number one priority. Now more than ever there has been lots of violence, especially gun violence, at colleges across America and at some point people may be forced to put their safety over the cost of schools. I also wonder that if for this particular group, if you were to give the current 16 to 19 year olds the same survey when they're graduate students, how they would change after having collegiate experience.

This relates to me and my community because as a college student just a few years ago me and my peers were forced to answer these very questions when deciding out schools. For me, tution and class sizes played the biggest factors in my decision.

comments.raw_comment:
In the graph, I notice that for both 16-19 year olds and recent college graduates, the consensus most important aspect of choosing a college is the tuition fees and how affordable they are. I also notice that the biggest difference in opinions occur for class sizes. Graduated students appreciated the idea of smaller classes while the college students to be accept the idea of larger class and lecture halls. I notice that the younger participants prioritized being closer to home a lot more than the graduated students. Which possibly could be attributed to them being timid about having to be independent for the first time in their lives. 

I wonder if the same survey was given to the 16-19 year olds after they graduated, if their results would shift and be closer to the what the graduated students are now. I also wonder if the gap between safe campus and affordable tuition will close in the coming years as unfortunately the rate of violence at colleges, such as mass shootings, has become only an increasing threat to students. I wonder if this continues how it will effect student's priorities.

This directly relates to my community as being a college student these are all questions I was forced to ask myself very similar questions when choosing the university I wanted to attend. For me, affordable tuition and small class sizes ended up being my deciding factors in choosing Cal Poly.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I notice is that a safe campus, higher income potential, and affordable tuition are above average in relative importance for both recent college grads and incoming college students. These are important factors when it comes to deciding on what college to attend. I also notice how the importance of small class sizes greatly increases from incoming college students to graduates. I also noticed that the importance of being close to home becomes less important for graduates than for incoming students. I found it interesting to see different perspectives on certain college attributes before and after experiencing a University. I wonder how a student's college experience may influence these changes in priority importance. Additionally, I wonder if incoming students value sports and proximity to home because it was important in their high school years, and as a graduate those certain values become less important with time. I would find it interesting to see the differences in the importance of a college's social life or the size of the school. This relates to me because as a college student, I can already see the changes in my priorities of choosing a college as I go through the experience myself. Overall, a good title to reflect this would be “Rethinking College Priorities with Experience”.

Showing that financial considerations are a top priority for younger generations, especially given rising inflation. Next criteria show that proximity to family and small class sizes show the greatest disparity between the groups. Teenagers aged 16 to 19 place more importance on staying close to family, likely because they're accustomed to being around them and may not wish to venture too far for college. Safety on campus is another area where this younger group shows greater concern, possibly influenced by recent safety threats such as school shootings. This could indicate a shift toward prioritizing campus safety more than past generations. As a college student, I find myself understanding and agreeing with these priorities, recognizing how crucial financial considerations have become for students today. 
Title : "The College Dilemma – How Students Prioritize College Selection Criteria."

comments.raw_comment:
After observing the graph, I notice that the priorities of 16 to 19 year olds and recent college graduates are very different when it comes to the importance of class sizes and whether the college is near their family or hometown. On the other hand, both groups highly prioritize and equally agree about graduate’s higher income potential and affordable tuition. 
	I wonder why there is such a large difference in priority for small class sizes. 16 to 19 years ranked small class sizes over a quarter less in importance than recent college graduates. I question if this is due to the differences in experience with education in both groups. For instance, 16 to 19 year olds most likely only experienced small class sizes because they've never been at a large college. Conversely, recent college graduates have probably had experience with large lectures in college. 
	This relates to me and my community because I am a college student and nearly everyone else I know is one as well. However, me and my community fall into the group between 16 to 19 year olds and recent college graduates so our relative importance of different priorities may differ from these two groups. The priorities that they voted on are all things that I considered when I was deciding which college to go to. I find it quite interesting that when I was a in high school, I had very similar ratings as the 16 to 19 year olds surveyed.
	A catchy headline is “High Schoolers Vs College Graduates: How Their Priorities Change”.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that both groups tend to agree on the importance of college aspects, especially for the things that are really important to them. Both groups find affordable tuition, higher income potential, and a safe campus to be very important when choosing a college. I also notice that the biggest gaps in aspects which the two groups differ upon are being near family/hometown and small class sizes.

comments.raw_comment: "In the realm of college selection, high school students and recent graduates share common ground in valuing affordable tuition and post-graduation income potential, rated at more than 4x in relative importance. Recent graduates, with experience, rate campus safety slightly lower at 2x, perhaps reflecting increased confidence. I wonder why recent college graduates place less emphasis on the safety of the campus compared to high school students. Could it be because they have already experienced college life and feel more confident about their safety? Additionally, recent grads emphasize small class sizes at just over 1/2x, contrasting with high schoolers' rating below 1/4x. These insights not only highlight diverse priorities but also guide current college students. The trio of financial feasibility, post-grad prospects, and campus safety are crucial considerations, shaping informed decisions. The headline encapsulating these findings: "Prioritizing the College Search: What Matters Most to Future and Recent Grads!"."

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed when looking at the graph is that the two age groups share a relatively similar idea of importance level for affordable tuition and that graduates' higher income potential. It is definitely not ironic that the younger generations' most important priorities when choosing a college has to do with money. With inflation increasing the prices of a lot of things, it is not surprising that those going into college and just coming out of college are thinking that money is the most important priority (of these 8). The next thing I notice is that being near family or their hometown and small class sizes have the largest difference between the two groups. For being near family or hometown, 16- to 19-year-olds voted it more important compared to the recent college graduates. This could mean that before college, teenagers are used to being with family, so they don't want to go too far. I also see that the 16- to 19-year-olds group voted more importance for a safe campus than the recent college graduates. I wonder if that is because of recent events that threaten schools, like school shootings, students will start to prioritize a safe campus, more so than previous generations. As a second year in college, I am right between the two groups. I understand all their decisions and do agree that a lot of students consider money as a top priority. A headline could be "The College Dilemma – Where Do You Rank These College Criteria?"

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is the differences between what pre- and post-college students find important. The criteria more about the social aspects show a higher importance for 16-19-year-olds much more than for those who already graduated, such as near family or hometown and sports. Retrospectively, students appear to no longer prioritize these factors once they have experienced college. Instead, the post-graduates place larger importance on academic criteria like class size. I wonder how ‘relative importance’ is calculated. If the poll these people took used some 1-10 scale, is the average importance just considered 5? More clarity on what the scale is would help to contextualize the true value of these rankings. This is relevant to me as a college student because it helps me to have a better understanding of the things I should take advantage of that I will actually find importance in after graduating. Additionally, part of my community is the high school students I coach, who ask me many questions about choosing the right colleges. Now I can give them better information on how what criteria they find important right now may change and how that may impact their decisions.
Title: “High Schoolers vs. Alumni: Changing College Priorities”

comments.raw_comment:
I find it interesting how priorities in college selection evolve between the ages of 16-19 and post-graduation. I noticed a larger emphasis on campus life and extracurricular activities among younger individuals which likely suggests a desire for a vibrant social environment. For example, the 16-19-year-old group prioritized campus safety, sports, and proximity to their hometown much more than recent graduates. On the other hand, recent graduates prioritize factors like class size and institutional type, indicating a shift towards academic considerations and perhaps a deeper understanding of how these factors impact their learning experience.

One thing I wonder is why smaller class sizes matter more to recent graduates than to 16-to-19-year-olds when choosing a college. Why does experiencing college make smaller class sizes more desirable? Does this imply that students do better in smaller classes or enjoy them more? Could this be because 16-to-19-year-olds don’t have much experience with smaller class sizes or prefer larger classes for some reason? If so, why?

This graph highly relates to my community because I recently graduated high school and am currently enrolled in college. I have noticed that my priorities for education have shifted throughout college and I wonder if others in my community have had a similar shift.

Upon analyzing the graph, I noticed two prominent trends. Firstly, both younger and older individuals prioritize economical aspects when selecting a college, favoring cost-effective alternatives and considering future income potential post-graduation as well as affordable tuition. Secondly, younger respondents are not as willing to relocate away from family given the it is way more important to them for the college to be close to their hometown. This is probably due to the fact that since they are younger, college is more unknown to them, so they want as aspect of comfort, especially with their surroundings, while in college. One thing I wonder is why both age groups do not seem to note any significant level of importance on whether the college is public or not. This relates to me and my community because I am currently a 20 year-old in college, so comparing my ideals now vs. when I was 16-19 is very interesting. It also helps me understand what other individuals in my community appear to value compared to what I value as well as how my values have changed throughout my time in college so far.

comments.raw_comment: What I notice in this graph is first that there are differences in the priorities between college graduates and 16- to 19-year-olds. In regards to how they rate the importance of affordable tuition, income potential, campus safety, distance from home, racial and ethnic diversity, small class sizes, varsity sports, and whether the school is public or private. I notice that although they place nearly the same importance on categories such as affordable tuition, income potential, and racial and ethnic diversity the other categories differ much more. This is because the other categories tend to be more solid regarding your outlook regardless of experience. 16- to 19-year-olds showed that they much more value living near home, while graduates do not since graduates would no longer be as dependent on their parents. Then regarding class sizes the 16 to 19-year-olds aren't as aware of the importance of the small class sizes that the graduates get to experience and value. I wonder why whether the school is public or private does not have more importance since that is also partially tied to whether the tuition is affordable. The impact this has on my community is that this can be used as help when deciding since you can look at the way someone who's experienced college follows things to draw from. It could impact your decisions or rank of colleges. I was once in the boots of the pre-graduates making that choice. A fitting title would be "Pre and Post College: Differing Priorities".

comments.raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed about this graph is that affordable tuition is by far the highest priority when choosing a college for both 16 to 19 year olds and recent college graduates. This is not super surprising, since most people probably want to pay as little as possible for college while also receiving quality education. I also noticed that affordable tuition, graduates' higher income potential, and racial/ethnic diversity are the only three factors that seem to be relatively agreed upon by both age groups. For the most part, there are fairly drastic differences in the opinions of what matters for both groups of people. Something I wonder about the graph is why it seems that neither age group has much care for whether or not a school is private. In general, private schools are much more expensive than public schools, and I would have thought that this would be a high concern when choosing a college. This part of the graph also seems to somewhat contradict the high value people are placing on the importance of affordable tuition. As a college student myself, this graph is relative to me and my community. As a sophomore in college, it was not too long away that I had to take all of the factors in the graph into consideration for myself, so it is very easy for me to form my own opinions on what I think is important for students choosing their future college. A catchy title for this graph might be "Collegiate Criteria- Factors to Consider Before Clicking 'Accept'".

I notice that there are some factors teens (aged 16-19 years) prioritize more than recent college graduates and vice versa. Some of these include a safe campus, how near the campus is to their hometown, and varsity sports importance. comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

Both 16-19 year olds and college graduates value affordable tuition and graduates higher income potential as their highest priorities. Other than those two instances of agreements, racial and ethnic diversity is considered important to both, and slightly more to college graduates. In order of how much the answers between both groups vary: Safe campus/Public or private, importance of varsity sports, near family, and class size. 

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder if the things that younger kids value - sports and family - change because college kids become more independent. Those who do not pursue sports as a career path may find that they do not have enough time to compete at the varsity level during completion of their degree. I wonder if also the experience of being on campus and in classes changed the minds of college graduates on how important the type, safety, and size of classes are for a university.


3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

As a junior who will be applying to college soon, I find myself aligning with the 16-19 year old opinion for the first 5 priorities (top to bottom), and the last three with recent college graduates. I’m sure that my opinions will change, but I know that I do value tuition and diversity the most personally. 

4. What's going on in this graph, create a catchy headline.

We want you! Priorities of pre and post college students.

Varsity sports are not very significant teens or recent college graduates but they are slightly more important to teens. Whether the school is public or private barely matters to either age group but are more important to recent college graduates. As someone who is 16 I agree with the relative importance that my age group chose with these topics and I will definitely be considering the when I choose a college to attend.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph compares the reasons why recent college graduates and 16- to 19-year-olds may choose a particular college. The graph's priorities range from financial concerns to the importance of whether the school is private or public. I noticed both 16 to 19-year-olds and recent college graduates place a high value on affordable tuition and potential earnings in the desired career after graduation. The most interesting difference I discovered was that recent college graduates valued being close to family and their home more than 16-19 year olds. Because of immaturity I would expect teens to want to stay close to home compared to young adolescents. I'm wondering how covid may have influenced these statistics. I'm curious if recent college graduates want to stay close to home because during their early college years spent at home caused them to want to go back, as opposed to younger high school students who felt trapped with their parents and wanted to get away.

This has an impact on my community because I am a senior in high school applying to college, and this graph helps me realize that students all over l have the same concerns as I do when it comes to college.

comments.raw_comment:
This is a graph that lists priorities for college students. The surveyors who created the graph compared the college priorities between 16-19 year olds and recent college graduates. Both groups seem to have similar wants, except in a few specific instances. The two topics where teens and graduates differ are class sizes and whether college is close to family. High schoolers value closeness to their family more than graduates. This likely because these students still live with their parents, and it's harder for them to imagine a college experience far away from their home. The other topic where the two subject groups differ is how important small class sizes are. Teens place class size importance low, while graduates place it at about average. This is probably because college students have had experience with the effects of different class sizes during their college education. 
I wonder where this study was conducted. I think it was probably conducted in the USA, based on how important affordable tuition is to these people. American colleges have very expensive tuition fees compared to other countries. If it wasn't done in America, then I don't think affordable tuition would be as prioritized.
I find this research to be informative. I didn't know that class size was really important. I'll definitely keep it in mind when I choose my own college.

comments.raw_comment: The graph compares the priorities of 16 to 19 year-olds and recent college graduates in selecting a college. From the data in the graph, I noticed that the 16 to 19-year olds and the college graduates were equally concerned about money. This is because affordable tuition and graduate’s higher income potential are prioritized in the graph. This may signify that both groups realistically consider how college can impact an individual’s life in the future–either because of loans or job opportunities and salaries. Additionally, I observed that a similar trend (when the 16 to 19-year olds and the college graduates agree on college factors) occurs in regards to racial and ethnic diversity at school. Furthermore, I noted that the largest disparity between the recent college graduates and the 16 to 19 year-olds is small class sizes. From the information in the graph, I wonder how the enrollment in state and community colleges is impacted. Also, I am curious whether the study was conducted in the United States, or did it involve college graduates and potential college students from other countries? The graph ultimately relates to my community as I am heading to college in the near future, as well as many of my classmates. When choosing a college, we will have to decide what factors to prioritize. Moreover, a headline that captures the main idea of the graph is “Weighing the Costs of College.”

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the prospective students favored how colleges would support their futures over anything else. The top priorities are safety, post-graduation income, and affordable tuition are some of the most important things for students after they graduate. They want to set themselves up for success by looking for a school that will keep them from harm and set them up to be financially stable. With inflation and the lack of economic stability that many high schools are seeing and experiencing, money remains a prevalent topic in college decisions. As a current senior, money and how a college will support my future have been very important to me. It is important to know that we will come out of school ready to start our professional lives, so it makes sense that money would be a majority interest for both recent graduates and current students. A headline for this graph could be "How the Priorities of Young People Before and After Graduation"

comments.raw_comment: The graph depicts the priorities of individuals when choosing a college. To do so, the 16- to 19-year-old and recently graduated college age brackets are examined. I notice that both groups of individuals prioritized three components on a similar scale: affordable tuition, graduates' higher income potential, and racial/ethnic diversity. The category with the largest deviation between levels of prioritization is class size. Recent college graduates factored small class sizes into the college decision process more than the 16- to 19-year-old age bracket. I wonder if there is a leading cause that resulted in the differences between categories that were prioritized. I also wonder why varsity sports and public or private school are not largely considered, as I would have thought these were factors more heavily taken into analysis. This impacts my community because it is a process that my classmates and I are currently going through. As seniors in high school, we must reflect on these factors while choosing a college. I would title this graph “Factors for Finding the College Fit.”

What do you wonder?

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me because I’m currently applying to college and considering all of these factors, I agree with most of the rankings of the 16-19 years old, who are my age range.

This relates to me and my community because I am about to be 16, and I am beginning to indulge in the college application process. These priorities are also some I will keep in mind as I begin looking into colleges in the near future. My catchy tite is Open Your Eyes and Prioritize.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph depicts what are the priorities that students ages 16-19 look and recent college graduates, when choosing what college to go to. I notice that the main or top priority for 16-19 year olds and recent college graduates are ones that deal with finances such as affordable tuition and the graduate's higher income potential. I notice that neither of the groups prioritize whether the college is public or private school which shows that they may not have a specific preference or simply are not looking for that. I wonder why small class sizes is not that high of a priority to students. Maybe they believe that learning in a larger environment is more beneficial to learn in compared to a smaller environment. Also, despite the age and grade difference the 16-19 year olds have similar priorities as do recent college graduates which shows that these priorities determine the perfect fit for a prospective student at a college. This relates to me and my community because I go to a private school and I am applying to colleges next year and these priorities are things that I need to look at when deciding what colleges I want to apply to, visit, see myself at, etc. Also, I attend a private school and the environment is intense when applying to colleges.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph compares the priorities of 16 to 19-year-olds and recent college graduates on why they may choose a certain college—priorities listed on the graph range from financial queries to the importance of sports to class size. As seen, both 16 to 19-year-olds and recent college graduates hold high priority in affordability and potential income in the workforce after graduating college. The biggest difference according to this graph is the concern about class size. Both groups have low concern if class sizes are small or not, recent college graduates fall just above ½ relative importance while 16 to 19-year-olds dip between ¼ to ⅛. I wonder if COVID has a role in this. Do the upcoming classes face the lingering effects of isolation because of the pandemic? Thus, are striving for larger class sizes to be surrounded by the people who were once taken away from their everyday lives? Another category that stuck out to me was the importance of campus safety. 16 to 19-year-olds are shown to value campus safety more than recent college graduates. I wonder if this is because of the increasing cases of violence on school grounds. In my community, most students I know have faced threats of weapons in school. Last May, my school had a three-hour lockdown after rumors of a suspected armed man circulated. Many kids I know, even my cousins as young as 10, talk of fear of gun violence on school grounds. 

“Safety, Sports, Size: The Priorities of College Life."

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?

Affordable tuition and high income potential are the most sought after and consistent factors in choosing a college for both 17-19 year old students and graduate students. The least considered factor is whether a school is private or public. However, graduates find the public/private factor more important than undergraduates. The most drastic differences are in class size and location relative to home. After graduating, it seems that people find more importance in small class sizes and less importance in distance from home.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why, after graduating, people find less importance in proximity to their hometown. Perhaps it’s because undergrads find that they won’t be able to establish a proper livelihood far from home, but once they have established this (by the time they graduate), they realize that it was never a really large issue.

What impact does this have on you and your community?

This helps me in my college choosing decisions, especially when looking at the importance of small class sizes, affordable tuition, and potential for high income. This graph, like with me, can help many other high school students engage in the tedious process of finding colleges that fit them. Reducing student stress and anxiety, this graph has a largely positive impact on students.

Headline:

Cracking the College Code: A Comparative Analysis of Student Priorities - Undergrads vs. Grad Students

The most important thing for sixteen to nineteen-year-olds and recent college graduates is money-related, affordable tuition and graduates' higher income potential are by far the two most important variables when selecting a college for both age groups. Both groups have similarly prioritized racial and ethnic diversity. For sixteen to nineteen-year-olds a safe campus, being near family or hometown, and varsity sports are more important to them than college graduates. College graduates prioritize small class sizes and whether the school is private or public. 

I wonder how the poll was conducted. I also wonder what would be the explanation of why one criterion was chosen over the others and vice versa. 

This relates to me and my community because choosing the right college is something that a lot of high school students are preparing for and actively looking forward to. I am a high school student who is considering college, looking at what other people want in a college helps me consider what I would want to consider myself.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is comparing the priorities of 16-19 year olds versus recent college graduates when it comes to choosing a college. When looking at the graph, I noticed that the factors where the two different age groups had the most similar opinions/agreed the most with one another were affordable tuition, graduates’ higher income potential, and racial and ethnic diversity as there are the smallest gaps between the two dots representing the two age groups for these three categories. Additionally, I noticed that the factor with the most relative importance was affordable tuition, which was way above average, whereas the two factors with the least relative importance were varsity sports being important and whether the school is public or private. The two factors that had the biggest discrepancies between the two age groups were the college being near family or one’s hometown and small class sizes. I wonder what causes these differences in scores and think it may be based on college graduates having actual experience at the college to base their opinions off of. This relates to my community because I, along with my peers, are in the process of applying to colleges and many of these factors are important to me when considering which schools to apply to. My headline for this graph would be: “Variations in College Priorities Before v. After Attending”.

comments.raw_comment:
1)The graph reveals that 16-19 year olds and recent graduates have different preferences when choosing a college. Recent graduates prefer colleges with small class sizes, while 16-19 year olds prioritize colleges near family or hometown. Both groups have similar views on affordable tuition, income potential, and racial and ethnicity. The older group focuses on the overall college experience, while the younger group is more interested in proximity, varsity sports, and school type.2) I wonder if having more experience causes college graduates to react differently from those in the 16–19 age range and similarly to one another. I'm also curious as to why they decided to reorder their priorities and if their thinking at that age was similar to that of the 16–19 age group.
3) This speaks to me and the community, I believe, because many individuals will know what to look for when choosing the kind of college they want to attend after seeing data about the top priorities in college selection. This helps us understand whether or not a college is the right choice for a particular person, as this depends on a variety of aspects, including the one shown in the graph. In particular, it provides me with options that address any issues I may have in selecting a college based on my priorities.
4)What should we prioritize when thinking about College?

1. It is illustrated that 16-19 year olds hold importance to the smaller things at colleges compared to college graduates. Also I know that with out of state colleges you would have to pay out of state tuition which is most likely higher than any home state tuition so logically it would make sense for 17-19 year olds to consider that as important.

College Experience and Lack Thereof - Perspectives from Both Sides

I noticed that the two groups are in agreement mostly for every priority, and that there is no major difference. It's interesting that every priority is thought of as less important than the average except for the first three ones. In fact, the first three aspects are agreed upon the most by the two groups, and they are all similar in the way that they affect the student's life the most directly. Affordable tuition and higher income potential are two large factors in someone's career. The rest of the priorities are important in the aspect of quality of life.
